extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners in philosophy, psychology, and the scientific study of human character
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological criteria for creating and evaluating Ethology — the deductive science of the formation of character built upon psychological laws. Emphasizes how to derive, verify, and responsibly apply causal laws about human character from empirical observation and psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from causal (explanatory) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: An Empirical Law is a uniformity true within observed limits but not guaranteed beyond them; causal laws are the principles that explain empirical generalizations and thereby delimit their applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws are 'approximate generalizations' dependent on particular conditions. Scientific work should seek the causal laws that explain empirical laws, because only then can we know the limits in which an empirical generalization may be relied on. Examples discussed: the Psalmist's hasty generalization that 'all men are liars', and age-related maxims (old cautious, young impetuous) which require causal explanation (experience, strength of inclination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the Deductive Method for highly complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: For phenomena of high complexity (e.g., formation of character), the Deductive Method — deriving consequences from general laws and verifying them by experience — is the proper logical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the character of an individual and the circumstances forming it are extremely complex, direct experiment or simple observation is inadequate; deduction from simpler, established laws (psychology) is the practicable route. The text: 'Deductive Method, setting out from general laws, and verifying their consequences by specific experience, is alone applicable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of experimentation and direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essentially impossible to study formation of character by fully controlled experiments or by completely accurate observation of all relevant impressions and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid experiment would require recording every sensation and impression from infancy onward — practically impossible. Observational studies are rough and 'en masse' and miss many influencing circumstances; single actions or short behaviors are poor indicators of character. Anti-pattern: treating limited, uncontrolled observations as definitive causal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethological propositions should assert tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about causes in Ethology must express tendencies (what a cause tends to produce) rather than categorical universal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'bodily strength tends to make men courageous', 'experience tends to give wisdom'. Propositions are valid as long as they assert effects 'so far as [a cause] operates uncounteracted.' Do not claim inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify theoretical deductions against empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions from general laws should be compared with empirical laws collected from observation as a form of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of deduction must be followed by verification against observed regularities ('compare the results of deduction... with general propositions expressive of the points of agreement which have been found among many instances'). Historical example: Newton using Kepler's empirical laws to verify his theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize simplest cases (fewest causes) for inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking causal laws by induction, begin with the simplest cases in which the fewest causes operate; these cases are most amenable to induction and often yield the most general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler cases allow more complete realization of inductive conditions. The simplest cases, being those in which fewest causes are simultaneously concerned, 'will be most amenable to the inductive process; and these are the cases which elicit laws of the greatest comprehensiveness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and value intermediate principles (axiomata media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle-level causal principles (axiomata media) are especially valuable for practical science because they bridge general laws and empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These middle principles are often the most useful for explaining and predicting complex phenomena. The text notes Bacon's emphasis on axiomata media but cautions that the method of arriving at them may be deductive as well as inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require sufficiently numerous and comparable instances for empirical verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical verification requires large and fairly selected samples so comparisons can eliminate chance and isolate the influence of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons should be of ratios/degrees across sufficiently many cases (example: fair samples of 100 Frenchmen vs 100 Englishmen ranked by a trait). Small or poorly selected samples do not constitute real induction and are unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overgeneralize empirical maxims beyond their original conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical maxims valid in one time, place, or social context cannot be safely transferred to another without showing the underlying causal conditions are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims collected from Englishmen may fail for Frenchmen, or present-day observations may not apply to past or future generations. To apply a maxim elsewhere, resolve it into the causes that produce it and verify those causes obtain in the new context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze complex phenomena by composition from simpler laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand formation of character, deduce the effects of assumed sets of circumstances from the general (psychological) laws of mind that compose the complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethology should 'try its experiments not on the complex facts, but on the simple ones of which they are compounded' — ascertain the laws of the constituent causes and infer the complex outcomes by composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple causal sources for individual differences (mental history and organic conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations of differences in minds should consider (1) original predispositions, (2) previous mental history (habits, education), and (3) varieties of physical/organic organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: differing intensity of desire may arise from nervous susceptibility which intensifies sensation, thereby producing stronger mental responses without direct physical causation of desire; instincts likely have a direct organic connection but may be modified by education. Avoid attributing all differences to unanalyzable 'ultimate facts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for pervasive modifying causes and contingency in predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that innumerable surrounding facts influence mental development, so predictions about character must be probabilistic and limited to tendencies under given (unfrustrated) conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if few simple laws determine mind, the sheer number of modifying circumstances makes precise prediction impracticable. Ethological laws are valuable when they indicate tendencies that can be used to shape circumstances toward desired ends, even without perfect prediction.
